passage:
First Monday: Jaya, nineteen, forwarded a video to the family group: a crowd, dramatic music, a caption claiming a whole community had attacked a temple. Within minutes her aunt Hansa replied, "Beta, this is from another country, three years old." Jaya felt her face burn and deleted it.

The next Wednesday: In her college media class, the teacher played the same clip without music. It looked like an ordinary street scuffle. Jaya wrote in her notebook: "Music = telling me what to feel."

Three weeks later: Before sharing anything, she searched for the original source and read at least one article from people she usually disagreed with. Over tea, she told Hansa, "Their argument on the water tax actually made sense. I still don't agree on the rest." Hansa smiled into her cup.

qa.q: How old was the video Jaya forwarded, according to Hansa?
qa.a: It was three years old and from another country.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel when her aunt pointed out the video was fake?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed, which is why her face burned and she quickly deleted it.

qa.q: Which new habit protects Jaya best, and why?
qa.a: Checking the original source before sharing, because it stops her from spreading misleading clips built to stir emotions.

qa.q: How might Hansa see the change in her niece over those weeks?
qa.a: She seems quietly pleased that Jaya now weighs other views fairly and doesn't just react to dramatic videos.

grounding: Shows over weeks a young adult learning to spot emotional manipulation and misinformation and to consider opposing views fairly.

passage: Sachin set down his tea. "Kamal, before you share that, sit down. Let me tell you about a morning when I was a young reporter in our town. A rumour spread that someone had poisoned the well near the market. By noon people were gathering with sticks, and every version of the story blamed a different family. I was your age, heart pounding, notebook in hand. My editor said, 'Find who saw it. Not who heard it.' I walked to the well. The water had turned cloudy from a broken pipe. That was all. We printed it, and the crowd went home. Since then I've read two newspapers every morning, one I like and one that annoys me. The annoying one keeps me honest. Now, where did your clip come from?"

qa.q: What did Sachin's editor tell him to find?
qa.a: Who saw it, not who heard it.

qa.q: What does Sachin think Kamal might be about to do, and why does that worry him?
qa.a: He thinks Kamal is about to share a clip without checking it, and he worries because he has seen how fast rumours can stir angry crowds.

qa.q: What would Sachin advise Kamal to do with the clip?
qa.a: Trace it back to someone who actually saw the event, and look at other sources, including ones he disagrees with, before sharing.

qa.q: How might the family that was blamed have felt if the rumour hadn't been checked?
qa.a: They could have faced fear and violence for something that never happened, so the checking protected innocent people. 🙏

grounding: An elder tells a young adult how checking facts stopped a dangerous rumour and why he reads opposing views.

passage: Anirban had two hours to submit his assignment: evaluate a viral post claiming a new city law would ban street vendors. The hostel Wi-Fi had died, so he and Santosh squeezed into a noisy cybercafe with a flickering monitor. The post used a crying vendor's photo and bold red letters. Anirban's first reaction was anger. Then he paused. "Why is it so loud?" he muttered. He found the actual draft law on the municipal site. It proposed vending zones, not a ban. He also opened a column from a vendors' union arguing the zones were too far from customers. Their point seemed fair. With twenty minutes left, he wrote: the post was misleading, but the worry behind it deserved a real hearing. Santosh read it over his shoulder. "Balanced, man."

qa.q: What did the actual draft law propose?
qa.a: It proposed vending zones, not a ban.

qa.q: Why did Anirban pause after his first angry reaction?
qa.a: He noticed the post seemed designed to stir emotion, which made him suspicious and want to check.

qa.q: Which part of Anirban's approach was most fair-minded?
qa.a: He checked the real law but still took the vendors' union's concern seriously, instead of dismissing one side.

qa.q: How might a vendor reading Anirban's conclusion feel?
qa.a: They might feel their worry was respected, even though the scary claim of a ban was shown to be false.

grounding: Shows a young adult under time pressure identifying misinformation while fairly weighing an opposing view.

passage:
Kiran (landlord): Hi Samir. From next month the rent goes up. New amount attached.
Samir: Hi uncle, thanks for telling me early. That's a big jump for me as a student 😬
Kiran (landlord): Prices have gone up everywhere.
Samir: I understand. Could we meet halfway? I pay a smaller increase now, and I sign for two years instead of one.
Kiran (landlord): Two years?
Samir: Yes. You won't need to find a new tenant or repaint. I've paid on time for 11 months.
Kiran (landlord): That's true. You're a good tenant.
Samir: I can also fix the balcony latch myself, I know it's been loose.
Kiran (landlord): Hmm. Let me think tonight.
Kiran (landlord): OK. Smaller increase, two-year agreement. Send me the draft.
Samir: Thank you uncle 🙏 I'll send it tomorrow.

qa.q: For how many months had Samir paid rent on time?
qa.a: For 11 months.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling on first reading the rent message?
qa.a: Samir was worried and a bit stressed, since the increase was a big jump for a student.

qa.q: Which move helped Samir reach a deal, and why?
qa.a: Offering a longer agreement, because it gave the landlord stability and saved him trouble, so both sides gained.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Samir by the end of the chat?
qa.a: As a reliable tenant worth keeping, which is why he agrees to the smaller increase.

grounding: Shows a young adult advocating for themselves in a rental negotiation and finding a compromise that benefits both sides.

passage: In the kasba market, Minakshi, twenty-one, set her basket of homemade mango pickle jars on Saurabh's shop counter. He picked one up and sniffed. "Good. But I can only pay this much." He named a price below what the oil and mangoes had cost her. Minakshi's jaw tightened. She had practised this with her mother. "Bhaiya, at that price I lose money. But if you take twenty jars a month instead of five, I can come down a little." Saurabh frowned. "And if they don't sell?" "Put them near the billing counter. If they're still here after a month, I'll take back what's left." He looked at the jars, then at her steady face. "Fine. Twenty jars. Your price minus a bit." She walked out, heart racing, grinning.

qa.q: What did Minakshi sell to Saurabh's shop?
qa.a: Homemade mango pickle jars.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's tightened jaw suggest when she heard his first price?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and firm, because his offer was below what the ingredients had cost her.

qa.q: What made Minakshi's counter-offer work?
qa.a: She traded a small price cut for a larger order and offered to take back unsold jars, easing his risk while protecting her income.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see the deal afterwards?
qa.a: He probably feels he got a fair price with little risk, and may respect Minakshi for negotiating calmly.

grounding: Shows a young woman in a small town negotiating a mutually beneficial deal for her homemade goods.

passage: In a café in Amsterdam, Bilal, twenty-two, a freelance graphic designer, sat across from his client Yosef, who ran a small bakery chain. Yosef slid over a list: a new logo, menus, signboards, and social media posts every week. "For the same price we agreed," he added. Bilal felt the old urge to just say yes so he wouldn't lose the job. He took a breath. "I really want to work on this," he said. "But the extra posts are a whole second job. I can do the logo, menus and signs for the agreed price. The weekly posts, I can offer as a monthly package, or train someone on your team to do them." Yosef tapped his cup. "Train someone. That's smart." They shook hands on it, and Bilal updated the contract that evening.

qa.q: What kind of business did Yosef run?
qa.a: A small bakery chain.

qa.q: What was Bilal afraid of when he saw the longer list?
qa.a: He was afraid of losing the client, so he felt the urge to say yes to everything.

qa.q: How did Bilal's reply protect his interests while keeping the client happy?
qa.a: He showed enthusiasm, clearly separated what was agreed from the extra work, and offered useful alternatives.

qa.q: What would change if Bilal had just agreed to everything?
qa.a: He would likely end up overworked and underpaid, and might come to resent the job and Yosef. 😓

grounding: Shows a young freelancer advocating for fair terms and reaching a compromise in a contract discussion.

passage:
Dear Sudha aunty,

I got the Bengaluru job. I start in three weeks. I'm writing because when I tried to tell Amma on the phone, I started laughing and then crying at the same time, and she got confused.

I'm so excited. My own salary, my own room, a city where nobody knows me as "the quiet girl from the corner house". I keep imagining walking to work with a coffee like in films.

And I'm terrified. I've never cooked a full meal. I've never taken a bus alone at night. What if I'm lonely? What if I fail and have to come back?

Both feelings sit together and neither one leaves. Is that normal? You moved to Delhi at my age. Did you feel like this?

Your Manjula

qa.q: How many weeks until Manjula starts her new job?
qa.a: She starts in three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Manjula laugh and cry at the same time on the phone?
qa.a: She feels thrilled about her new independence and scared of the unknowns, and both feelings came out together.

qa.q: What could Sudha aunty say to help her niece?
qa.a: That holding both feelings is normal, and share how she herself managed her first months in a new city. 🙂

qa.q: How might Amma have felt hearing her daughter laugh and cry at once?
qa.a: Confused and probably a little worried, unsure whether Manjula was happy or upset.

grounding: A young woman writes about feeling excitement and fear together as she prepares for independence.

passage: Uday pulled his knees up on the bench. "So Rekha, you asked why I've been weird all week. Okay. The hostel allotment came through. I leave home on Sunday. And honestly? I can't tell if I want to run or hide. One minute I'm planning posters for my room, thinking, finally, no curfew, no Papa asking where I'm going. The next minute I'm standing in the kitchen watching Ma make parathas and I get this lump in my throat. Who'll make me tea when I'm sick? What if nobody talks to me? And then I feel guilty for being excited to leave them at all. Yesterday I packed my bag, unpacked it, then packed it again. My little brother thinks I've lost it. Maybe I have. Both feelings are just... there, at the same time."

qa.q: On which day does Uday leave home?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: Why does Uday feel guilty about being excited?
qa.a: He loves his family and worries that looking forward to leaving means he doesn't care about them enough.

qa.q: What small step could help Uday with his mixed feelings?
qa.a: Saying them out loud to someone like Rekha, as he is doing, and planning regular calls home so leaving feels less like a loss.

qa.q: How might Uday's little brother see him packing and unpacking?
qa.a: He seems puzzled and thinks Uday has lost it, maybe not realising his brother is torn between excitement and fear.

grounding: A young man tells a friend about holding excitement for independence and fear of leaving home at once.

passage: My sister Jaya leaves for her master's in Germany next week, and our flat is a mess of suitcases. I've been watching her. Yesterday she spent an hour on the phone with her future flatmate, laughing loudly, planning weekend trips to lakes. Then she hung up and sat on the floor next to her open bag, very still, holding Ma's old shawl. When I asked if she was okay, she said, "Nikita, I'm so happy," and her eyes filled up. At dinner she joked about finally escaping my snoring. Later I heard her in the bathroom, crying quietly. This morning she was dancing to music while ironing. I don't really know what's going on inside her. Maybe it's everything at once. I'm going to miss her terribly.

qa.q: What was Jaya holding while she sat next to her bag?
qa.a: Ma's old shawl.

qa.q: What does Jaya saying 'I'm so happy' while her eyes filled up suggest?
qa.a: She seems to be feeling joy and sadness together, excited for her new life but sad to leave home.

qa.q: How could Nikita support Jaya in her last week at home?
qa.a: She could spend simple time with her, let her talk about both the fun plans and the fears, and plan how they'll stay in touch.

qa.q: What is it like for Nikita to watch her sister prepare to leave?
qa.a: She is trying to read Jaya's swings without really knowing her inner state, while dealing with her own sadness at losing her.

grounding: A younger sister describes a young adult showing excitement and fear together before moving abroad.

passage: "Saurabh, I went back to our old flat in Kolkata last week. Just stood outside. The building's been painted this weird green. The mango tree where we tied the cricket stumps is gone. And the tea stall uncle still recognised me! He said, 'Arnab babu, you've grown a beard.' I laughed and then had to turn away because my eyes were stinging. I kept thinking of summers when the only worry was whose turn it was to bat. Now it's rent, exams, job forms, Ma's health. Part of me wants to go back to being that nine-year-old, just for a day. But then I remember I also hated being told what to do all the time. It's weird. I miss it, and I'm glad it's over."

qa.q: What had happened to the mango tree outside Arnab's old flat?
qa.a: It was gone.

qa.q: Why did Arnab have to turn away at the tea stall?
qa.a: Being recognised brought back memories of his carefree childhood, and he felt a sudden rush of longing that made his eyes sting.

qa.q: What could Arnab do with this feeling instead of just aching?
qa.a: He could share memories with old friends like Saurabh or make small time for play, letting nostalgia comfort him without pulling him backward.

qa.q: How might the tea stall uncle have felt seeing Arnab again?
qa.a: He was probably happy and a bit amazed at how the boy had grown up, remembering him as a child in the lane.

grounding: A young man describes a bittersweet longing for the simple safety of his childhood while facing adult worries.

passage: During exam week, my roommate Aditi started doing strange things. I'm Pankaj, we share a study room in our college flat, and she's usually all planners and highlighters. But on Tuesday night I found her watching old cartoons we both grew up with, the theme song on repeat, eating the cheap orange candy we used to buy for one rupee. She'd found a packet at a shop near the station. When I teased her, she laughed and said, "Everything was simpler when this was my biggest problem." She said it lightly, but she didn't look at me. Later I saw her looking at a photo of her grandmother's house on her phone. I can't say for sure what she's feeling. Maybe it's the exams. Maybe she just misses being small.

qa.q: Where did Aditi find the orange candy?
qa.a: At a shop near the station.

qa.q: What does Aditi's comment about things being simpler suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She seems to be longing for the safety of childhood as a comfort against exam stress, though she says it lightly.

qa.q: How could Pankaj support Aditi without prying?
qa.a: Pankaj could join her for an episode, share some childhood memories of their own, and gently ask how she is coping with exams.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Aditi's change during exam week?
qa.a: Pankaj is surprised, since she is usually organised, and admits being unable to be sure what she's feeling.

grounding: A roommate describes a young adult seeking comfort in childhood memories and treats during stressful exams.

passage:
Before: The week before her family sold their old house, Ayesha, twenty, packed up her childhood room. She found her Class 4 diary under the bed: "Today Varun and I made a tent from bedsheets. Best day ever." She laughed, then sat on the floor for a long time.

During: On moving day she argued with Ammi about keeping a broken toy piano. "It's junk, Ayesha." "It's mine." She won. It went into the car, wrapped in a towel.

After: A month later in her college hostel, she pinned a photo of the old gate above her bed. She video-called Varun, now at university in another city. "Remember the bedsheet tent?" He groaned. "You're so dramatic." But he stayed on the call for an hour, talking about old summers.

qa.q: What did Ayesha and Varun make from bedsheets in Class 4?
qa.a: A tent.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha fight to keep the broken toy piano?
qa.a: It held memories of her childhood home, and letting it go felt like losing part of that safe, simpler time.

qa.q: What helped Ayesha carry her nostalgia into her new life in a healthy way?
qa.a: Pinning the photo and calling Varun let her keep the memories close and share them, instead of just grieving alone.

qa.q: How might Varun feel on the call, despite teasing her?
qa.a: He probably misses those summers too, since he stays on for an hour talking about them. 😊

grounding: Shows over weeks a young adult's bittersweet longing for childhood as the family home is sold.

passage:
Before: Francis, twenty-two, refreshed his email so often that his roommate hid his phone. The job offer from the design studio came on a Thursday. He shouted so loud the neighbour knocked.

During: Two weeks later he and his cousin Hansa went to look at a tiny one-room flat near the office. Peeling paint, a window facing a banyan tree. Francis walked around touching the walls. "My own kitchen," he kept saying. "Hansa, I'll cook here!" "You can't even make tea." "I'll learn!"

After: On his first morning at work, he woke before the alarm, ironed his shirt twice and reached the office forty minutes early. The security guard laughed at him. Francis didn't care. He sat on the steps with a sketchbook, drawing the street, humming.

qa.q: What faced the window of the one-room flat?
qa.a: A banyan tree.

qa.q: How can you tell Francis felt eager about his new adult life?
qa.a: He shouted at the offer, kept touching the walls of the flat, woke before his alarm and reached work forty minutes early.

qa.q: What could Francis do to keep his excitement from turning into disappointment?
qa.a: Enjoy it while expecting some bumps, like learning to cook step by step and asking for help at work when he needs it.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel watching Francis at the flat?
qa.a: Hansa teases him about his tea-making, but seems fond of his enthusiasm and happy for him.

grounding: Shows over weeks a young adult's forward-looking eagerness about a first job and first home.

passage: Rekha's grandfather Rafiq smiled and folded his newspaper. "Rekha beti, you ask what it felt like to start out? Let me tell you. I was twenty when I got the letter for the bus conductor's post in the city. I read it on the village well so many times the paper went soft. The night before I left, I couldn't sleep. I kept imagining the city lights, the uniform, my own salary in my own pocket. My mother packed rotis and pickle and cried. I was sad for her, but my chest felt like a kite pulling at its string. On the first morning I reached the depot before the manager. I polished my ticket punch until it shone. The job was hard, the hours long. But that feeling of the whole world opening up? I still remember it."

qa.q: What job did Rafiq get the letter for?
qa.a: A bus conductor's post in the city.

qa.q: What does Rafiq mean when he says his chest felt like a kite pulling at its string?
qa.a: He felt a strong, joyful pull toward the new life ahead, even while he was sad to leave his mother.

qa.q: What could Rekha take from her grandfather's story for her own future?
qa.a: That it's normal to feel eager and excited about new adult chances, even when the work turns out hard.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's mother have felt the night before he left?
qa.a: She was sad to see him go, as her crying shows, while perhaps also proud he had found work.

grounding: An elder recalls his eager, forward-looking excitement as a young man starting his first job in the city.

passage: The night before Hafsa left for her first job in the city, the monsoon broke. Water swirled ankle-deep in the lane, and the power went out at nine. Her mother fretted about the morning train. Her brother Suraj held a candle while Hafsa knelt beside her suitcase, packing by its wobbling light. She should have been worried. Instead she kept grinning. "Suraj, I'll have an ID card. With my photo. And a desk." "You'll have wet shoes first," he said. She laughed, wrapped her certificates in a plastic bag twice over, and wrote a list: umbrella, snacks, charger, courage. At four in the morning she was already dressed, standing at the door, listening to the rain, feeling like the whole of her life was about to begin.

qa.q: What did Hafsa wrap her certificates in?
qa.a: A plastic bag, twice over.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa keep grinning despite the storm?
qa.a: Her excitement about her new job and adult life was stronger than her worry about the flooding and the power cut.

qa.q: How could Suraj help his sister on the morning of the trip?
qa.a: He could help carry her bags through the water and make sure she reaches the station on time.

qa.q: What might Hafsa's mother be feeling that night?
qa.a: She seems anxious about the flood and the train, and perhaps also about her daughter leaving home.

grounding: Shows a young adult's eager anticipation of adult life shining through despite a stormy, difficult night.

passage:
Chinmay: bro I can't do this
Uday: what happened
Chinmay: Papa's in hospital since yesterday. doctors say he'll recover but it'll take time
Chinmay: I'm the only one here. there's forms, insurance papers, the landlord wants rent, and my joining date at work is Monday
Chinmay: I've been sitting in the corridor for 2 hours staring at my phone. I can't even start
Uday: ok. breathe. I'm coming after my shift
Uday: can you just write everything down? one list. don't solve it, just write it
Chinmay: ok
Chinmay: done. 7 things
Uday: pick the one that's due first
Chinmay: insurance form
Uday: do only that one. then call your HR, tell them what's happening
Chinmay: ...ok. hands still shaking
Uday: I'll be there by 8. bringing food 🤍

qa.q: How long had Chinmay been sitting in the hospital corridor?
qa.a: For 2 hours.

qa.q: Why couldn't Chinmay start on anything?
qa.a: So many serious responsibilities landed on Chinmay at once that Chinmay felt overwhelmed and frozen, not knowing where to begin.

qa.q: What small step did Uday suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Writing everything into one list and doing only the most urgent item, which broke the overwhelming pile into something manageable.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's HR team see him if he explains what's happening?
qa.a: They are likely to understand a family emergency and may offer flexibility, which could ease his worry about the joining date.

grounding: Shows a young adult paralysed by a sudden wave of adult duties, and a friend helping him take one step at a time.

passage: After her father fell ill last spring, Trisha, twenty-one, found herself running the family's grocery shop in the small town, while still finishing her BCom. Every evening she sat at the counter with the ledger, the bank loan letter, her little sister's school fee receipt and a list of suppliers to pay. One night she opened the ledger, stared at the columns and felt her whole body go still. The numbers blurred. A customer asked for sugar twice before she heard him. After closing, she sat on the step outside, not moving, while the street dogs settled down for the night. Her mother came out, sat beside her and said nothing for a while. Then: "Tomorrow, I'll handle the suppliers. You do only the bank." Trisha leaned against her shoulder.

qa.q: What did the customer ask Trisha for twice?
qa.a: Sugar.

qa.q: What does Trisha's stillness at the counter suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She was flooded by too many adult duties at once, so overwhelmed that she froze and couldn't take in what was around her.

qa.q: How did her mother's offer help, and what could come next?
qa.a: Splitting the tasks gave Trisha one clear job; next they could make a shared weekly plan so she isn't carrying everything alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Trisha's mother to see her daughter frozen on the step?
qa.a: She seems to understand without words and chooses quiet presence and practical help over questions.

grounding: Shows a young woman in a small town paralysed by a sudden load of permanent family responsibilities.

passage: In her first month living alone in Stockholm, Hana, twenty-two, stood in the supermarket unable to choose between two bags of rice. That morning she'd opened three letters: a tax registration form, a notice about her apartment lease, and a reminder about her work contract. Each needed something she didn't understand. Now even rice felt like a decision too big to make. She left the basket in the aisle and walked out. At home, she lay on the floor. Her friend Anders came by with cinnamon buns and found the letters on the table. "Okay," he said, spreading them out. "Which one has a date on it?" Only one did. They filled that form together. Hana cried a little, laughing at herself. "I couldn't even pick rice."

qa.q: How many letters did Hana open that morning?
qa.a: Three letters.

qa.q: Why could Hana not choose between the two bags of rice?
qa.a: She was so flooded by the unfamiliar adult tasks in the letters that even a small choice felt too heavy.

qa.q: What did Anders do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: He sorted the letters by which had a deadline, so Hana could focus on one task instead of all of them.

qa.q: How might Anders feel finding his friend on the floor?
qa.a: He is probably worried but calm, choosing practical help and company rather than making her feel foolish.

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad feeling paralysed by a sudden flood of adult paperwork and responsibilities.

passage: The waiting room outside the college sports physio smelled of antiseptic and old mats. Leela sat with her knee strapped, staring at the trophy cabinet. Two months ago she'd been picked for the state hockey camp, the first step toward the national team she'd trained for since she was twelve. Then the tackle. The torn ligament. The doctor's words that morning had been careful and kind: she'd walk and run again, but competitive hockey at that level probably wasn't coming back. Her teammate Gopika came in, sat down, and handed her a bottle of water. Leela said, "I don't even know who I am if I'm not that." Gopika didn't try to fix it. She just said, "You're still you," and stayed until the physio called her name.

qa.q: Where did Leela sit with her knee strapped?
qa.a: In the waiting room outside the college sports physio.

qa.q: What does Leela mean when she says she doesn't know who she is anymore?
qa.a: She is grieving not just the injury but the future and identity she had built around hockey since she was twelve.

qa.q: Why was Gopika's quiet presence helpful?
qa.a: She didn't rush to fix or minimise the loss, which let Leela feel her sorrow without being alone. 🤍

qa.q: How might the loss feel different for Gopika, who is still on the team?
qa.a: She may feel sad for her friend and perhaps a little guilty that her own path continues while Leela's has changed.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the loss of an idealised future after a career-ending injury.

passage:
Dear Bhaiya,

You asked why I've been quiet on calls. Meera and I broke up. Four years. It was mutual, which somehow makes it worse. Nobody did anything wrong. We just wanted different cities, different lives.

I keep reaching for my phone to tell her small things, like the new chai place near the office, and then I remember. I walk past our bench in the park and feel hollow. I had a whole future in my head: the flat, the dog, Sunday lunches with both families. Now that future is just gone, and I didn't know you could grieve something that never actually happened.

I'm okay, mostly. Going to work, eating. Just sad in a deep, slow way.

Come home for Diwali?

Tanvir

qa.q: How long were Tanvir and Meera together?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir feel the grief is for more than Meera herself?
qa.a: Tanvir is mourning the imagined future they had planned together, the flat, the dog, the family lunches, which now won't happen.

qa.q: What could Bhaiya do in reply?
qa.a: Call Tanvir, listen without trying to fix it, and make a plan to be together at Diwali as Tanvir asked. 🫂

qa.q: How might Meera be experiencing the same breakup?
qa.a: Since it was mutual, she may also be grieving the future they shared, even though she agreed it had to end.

grounding: A young adult writes about the deep sorrow of losing a long relationship and the future they had imagined.

passage: Dhruv rubbed his face with both hands. "Amandeep, you know how long I prepared for the army. Since Class 9. Morning runs, pushups on the terrace, the medical, the written test, the interview. I thought I'd done well. Yesterday the final list came out. My name wasn't there. And I'm over the age limit for trying again. That's it. Done. I didn't cry in front of Mummy. I went to the ground where I used to run and sat there till it got dark. It's not just the job, you know? It's the picture I carried of myself in uniform, making Papa proud. That picture's just... gone. I don't know what I want now. I'm not asking you to fix it. I just needed to say it out loud to someone."

qa.q: Since which class had Dhruv been preparing for the army?
qa.a: Since Class 9.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv go to the ground and sit there until dark?
qa.a: He was grieving deeply and needed a place to feel the loss privately, away from his mother.

qa.q: How could Amandeep best respond right now?
qa.a: By listening and staying with him instead of offering quick solutions, as Dhruv asked, and checking in over the next days.

qa.q: What would change if Dhruv's father were in the room hearing this?
qa.a: Dhruv might feel he had failed him, or he might realise his father cares about him more than the uniform.

passage: The rains failed that year. Minakshi, twenty, stood at the edge of her family's dry field outside the village, where the cotton plants had wilted before they flowered. She had planned to start college in the district town in July. Now there was no money for fees, and her father needed help with the goats and the dairy work. For weeks she'd been angry, checking the sky, refusing to talk about it. This evening her friend Parveen found her sitting on the field boundary. "What will you do?" Minakshi was quiet a long time. "Work this year. Save a little. Study from books at night. Go next year." She said it calmly. Parveen looked surprised. "You're not angry anymore?" "I'm tired of fighting the sky," Minakshi said, almost smiling.

qa.q: What crop had wilted in the family's field?
qa.a: The cotton plants.

qa.q: How had Minakshi's feelings changed by the evening Parveen found her?
qa.a: She had moved from weeks of anger to a calm acceptance of the situation and a practical new plan.

qa.q: What small step makes Minakshi's plan realistic?
qa.a: Studying from books at night while working and saving, which keeps her goal alive even with a delay.

qa.q: Why might Parveen react with surprise to Minakshi's calm?
qa.a: She had seen weeks of anger, so she expected more frustration, not a quiet plan.

grounding: Shows a young woman in a village accepting a hard reality after drought and adapting her plans.

passage: Marek, twenty-one, had spent a year planning to study in Canada. The visa rejection email arrived on a grey Tuesday in Warsaw. For a week he wrote appeal drafts at two in the morning, sure there must be a mistake. His flatmate Nkechi found him asleep on the keyboard. "Did you read what they said?" she asked gently. He had, many times. The rules were clear; he didn't qualify this year. On Sunday he closed the laptop and walked along the river. He let himself feel it: the disappointment, the embarrassment of having told everyone. Then he went home and looked at master's programmes in Poland and Germany. That evening he told Nkechi, "It's not what I wanted. But it's what's true." She nodded and put the kettle on.

qa.q: In which city did Marek receive the visa rejection?
qa.a: In Warsaw.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling during the week of late-night appeal drafts?
qa.a: He was in denial and desperate, hoping there was a mistake rather than facing the disappointment.

qa.q: What helped Marek move toward acceptance?
qa.a: Letting himself feel the disappointment on his walk and then looking at realistic options, instead of fighting rules that were clear.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have felt watching Marek's week?
qa.a: She was probably worried to find him asleep on his keyboard, and relieved when he began to accept it.

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad letting go of fighting a clear setback and accepting a changed situation.

passage:
Monday night.

Results came out. I missed the engineering entrance cutoff again, second time. Aadhya called, and I couldn't even speak properly.

Spent the evening lying on the roof, staring at the water tank, feeling like the biggest failure in the colony. Mummy left dinner outside my door. I didn't eat for a while.

Around eleven I finally opened my mock test sheets. And I saw it: maths was fine, physics was fine, chemistry was a disaster both years. It's not that I'm stupid. It's one subject I kept avoiding.

I'm going to try one more time. Not the same way. Chemistry first, every morning. I'll ask Aadhya's cousin for her notes.

I'm scared to fail again. But I'm more scared of never finding out.

Chetan

qa.q: Which subject did Chetan see was the weak one in both years?
qa.a: Chemistry.

qa.q: What does Chetan mean by being more scared of never finding out?
qa.a: Chetan is afraid of failing again, but would regret giving up more, so chooses to try instead of quitting.

qa.q: Which part of Chetan's new plan shows a lesson learned from the setback?
qa.a: Tackling chemistry first every morning, because it targets the actual reason for missing the cutoff.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when Chetan says they're trying again?
qa.a: Aadhya would probably be relieved and proud after hearing Chetan unable to speak on the phone, and glad to help with the notes.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows the writer finding the grit to try again after a major setback, with a smarter plan.

passage: At the village akhada, the red earth was still marked from yesterday's district bout. Vijay, twenty-one, had lost in the final round, pinned in under a minute in front of the whole village. That night he didn't go home. He sat by the pit until his coach, Omkar ustad, found him. "Shame?" asked Omkar. Vijay nodded. "Everyone saw." "Everyone saw you get there too," Omkar said. "Why did you lose?" Vijay thought. "I rushed. I got tired too early." "So?" Vijay stood up, brushed the earth off his legs. "So I train stamina. Morning runs to the canal and back." At dawn the next day, the village milkman saw him running past the fields, alone, his breath clouding in the cold.

qa.q: Where did the milkman see Vijay running at dawn?
qa.a: Past the fields.

qa.q: How was Vijay feeling after losing the bout?
qa.a: He felt ashamed because the whole village had watched him lose.

qa.q: What did Omkar's questions help Vijay do?
qa.a: They helped him find the real reason he lost and turn his shame into a concrete training plan.

qa.q: How might the milkman see Vijay running alone at dawn?
qa.a: He might be surprised and impressed that the boy who lost is already back at work.

grounding: Shows a young wrestler in a village finding the grit to train again after a public defeat.

passage: Minakshi, twenty-two, had been teaching at the small-town government school for a year, and lately she'd stopped smiling. Lesson plans, inspections, parents at the gate. One Friday evening, as she walked home past the school ground, a group of kids and a few young men were playing kabaddi in the dust. Her cousin Nilesh waved. "Didi, we're one short!" She laughed and shook her head, but he wouldn't stop calling. She tucked her dupatta, kicked off her sandals and joined in. Within minutes she was shouting "kabaddi, kabaddi" and tagging two boys before getting caught, laughing so hard she had to sit down. Walking home with dusty feet, she realised her shoulders didn't ache for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What game were the kids and young men playing?
qa.a: Kabaddi.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's laughter and relaxed shoulders suggest about her?
qa.a: She had been carrying a lot of stress, and play let her release it and feel light again.

grounding: Shows a young teacher rediscovering play as a relief from work stress in her small town.

passage: In Lagos, Chidi, twenty-two, a junior nurse on night shifts, had started to feel like a machine. Work, sleep, work. His sister Ada noticed he'd stopped telling jokes at dinner. One Saturday she dragged him to an afrobeat dance class at a community hall. "I can't dance," he protested. "Nobody here can," she said. The instructor had them copying moves that made everyone look silly. Chidi tripped over his feet, bumped into Ada, and burst out laughing for the first time in weeks. By the end, he was sweaty and grinning. On the bus home, he found himself humming the music. "Same time next week?" Ada asked. "Only if you promise to look as bad as me," he said.

qa.q: Where was the dance class held?
qa.a: At a community hall.

qa.q: What might Chidi have been feeling before the class?
qa.a: He seemed drained and flat, like a machine, from constant work and night shifts.

qa.q: What small step helped Chidi feel lighter?
qa.a: Trying a playful, low-pressure activity with his sister where no one had to be good, which let him laugh again.

qa.q: How might Ada feel seeing her brother laugh again?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and happy, since she had noticed him stop joking and wanted him back. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad rediscovering play and humour as balance against work stress.
